messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Fisherman
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 65

He is a 58-year-old South Asian man who has spent most of his life on the water, working as a fisherman like his father before him. He speaks of the sea with a kind of respect that is almost personal, as if it has always been both provider and adversary. Before the accident, fishing is not just his job but the rhythm around which his life is built. His days begin before dawn, his hands accustomed to rope, net, salt, and weather, and his sense of himself is tied closely to being able to endure hard conditions without complaint. Since his wife died several years ago, he has lived more quietly, leaning on routine and the familiarity of work to keep his grief from feeling too large.

The accident happens during a routine outing that quickly turns dangerous when the boat is struck by sudden rough water and a loose line catches him at the wrong angle. In an instant, what should have been an ordinary day becomes a fight to survive. He is thrown hard, pinned, and nearly dragged under. He remembers the shock first: the burning pressure in his body, the salt in his mouth, the roar of water and metal, and the terrible certainty that he is going to die there, far from shore and alone. He describes the moment as stretching out endlessly, as if time slows enough for him to think of his wife and his children before everything narrows to panic. When he is finally pulled free, he is injured, shaking, and unable to stop trembling. Even after the immediate danger passes, his body continues to act as if the water is still around him.

In the weeks afterward, he tries to return to work, but the sea no longer feels familiar. What once gave him pride now triggers dread. The smell of diesel, the slap of waves against the hull, the sight of tangled rope, even the sound of a boat engine starting can make his chest tighten and his stomach drop. He begins to have intrusive images of the accident at odd moments, especially when he is alone or trying to sleep. At night, he wakes suddenly with his heart racing, convinced for a few seconds that he is back in the water. He avoids talking about what happened, even with family, because when he starts to describe it he feels the fear rise again in his throat and he worries he will lose control. He tells himself repeatedly that a man should be able to manage this, but the effort to stay composed leaves him exhausted.

He becomes increasingly cautious and tense on the water. He checks equipment over and over, scans the horizon constantly, and reacts sharply to unexpected movement. If a rope slips or a wave hits the side of the boat harder than usual, he flinches before he can stop himself. His concentration is worse, and he finds himself making small mistakes that would have been unthinkable before. At home, he sits in silence much of the time, distant from others and less interested in conversations he once would have joined. He feels irritable in ways that surprise him, especially when people ask questions he experiences as intrusive or when they suggest he should be “over it” by now. He does not like how often he feels on edge, as though danger might return at any moment.

Because he is widowed, there is no spouse at home to notice the changes first-hand or to help him settle at night. He manages largely on his own, though his adult children check on him and encourage him to rest. He accepts their concern but often keeps his distress hidden, wanting to remain the steady father they know. Still, they see that he is more withdrawn and less available than before. He continues to fish because it is the work he knows, and because stopping altogether feels like surrendering part of his identity. Yet each trip to sea costs him something: afterward he returns home drained, watchful, and more easily startled, with the day’s ordinary noises feeling louder than they should.

Over time, he begins to describe a life organized around bracing himself. He sleeps lightly, keeps his clothing and tools in specific places, and prefers predictable routes and routines. He rarely feels fully at ease, even on land. The memory of the accident is not only remembered but relived in sensations—wetness, pressure, breathlessness, the sharp expectation that something terrible is about to happen. He does not say much about fear, but it shows in the way he pauses before stepping onto the boat, in the way he grips railings a little too tightly, and in how quickly his face changes when anything reminds him of that day.
